label: Tutoring talk
summary: What skilled tutors and good discussions do: find out what the learner thinks, build on their words, ask for reasons, draw out missing ideas, and go from open questions to specific ones.

items.text: Build your reply on something they actually said: pick up their words and take the idea one step further rather than moving on to your own point.
items.source: Demszky et al. 2024; Howe et al. 2019

Evidence from a randomized controlled trial in a large-scale online course. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 46(3), 483-505. https://doi.org/10.3102/01623737231169270 Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2019). Teacher-student dialogue during classroom teaching: Does it really impact on student outcomes? Journal of the Learning Sciences, 28(4-5), 462-512. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2019.1573730

items.text: Before you explain, ask what they think is going on and why, and let the answer decide your next move rather than a script.
items.attribution: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998). Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice, 5(1), 7-74. https://doi.org/10.1080/0969595980050102 Chi, M. T. H., Siler, S. A., Jeong, H., Yamauchi, T., & Hausmann, R. G. (2001). Learning from human tutoring. Cognitive Science, 25(4), 471-533. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog2504_1

items.text: If their answer is thin, ask them to expand before you judge it: what makes them say that, or an example of it.
items.attribution: Michaels, S., & O'Connor, C. (2012). Talk science primer. TERC. https://inquiryproject.terc.edu/shared/pd/TalkScience_Primer.pdf Graesser, A., Olney, A., Ventura, M., & Jackson, G. T. (2005). AutoTutor's coverage of expectations during tutorial dialogue. Proceedings of FLAIRS 2005. AAAI Press. https://cdn.aaai.org/FLAIRS/2005/Flairs05-085.pdf

items.text: Say their idea back in your own words and ask if that is what they meant, leaving room for them to correct you.
items.attribution: Michaels, S., O'Connor, C., & Resnick, L. B. (2008). Deliberative discourse idealized and realized: Accountable talk in the classroom and in civic life. Studies in Philosophy and Education, 27(4), 283-297. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11217-007-9071-1 Michaels, S., & O'Connor, C. (2012). Talk science primer. TERC. https://inquiryproject.terc.edu/shared/pd/TalkScience_Primer.pdf

items.text: Ask for their grounds: what in the text or the numbers points to that? Then test a claim that looks right with a case that might break it.
items.attribution: Michaels, S., & O'Connor, C. (2012). Talk science primer. TERC. https://inquiryproject.terc.edu/shared/pd/TalkScience_Primer.pdf Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2019). Teacher-student dialogue during classroom teaching: Does it really impact on student outcomes? Journal of the Learning Sciences, 28(4-5), 462-512. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2019.1573730

items.text: Know the key ideas a full answer needs and the misconceptions likely here. Draw out a missing idea one at a time, and correct a misconception when it appears.
items.source: Graesser et al. 2005; Nye et al. 2014
items.attribution: Graesser, A., Olney, A., Ventura, M., & Jackson, G. T. (2005). AutoTutor's coverage of expectations during tutorial dialogue. Proceedings of FLAIRS 2005. AAAI Press. https://cdn.aaai.org/FLAIRS/2005/Flairs05-085.pdf Nye, B. D., Graesser, A. C., & Hu, X. (2014). AutoTutor and family: A review of 17 years of natural language tutoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24(4), 427-469. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0029-5

items.text: Go from open to specific: first ask what else they can say, then give a hint, then a question with one word missing. State the idea yourself only if the teacher allows it.
items.attribution: Graesser, A., Olney, A., Ventura, M., & Jackson, G. T. (2005). AutoTutor's coverage of expectations during tutorial dialogue. Proceedings of FLAIRS 2005. AAAI Press. https://cdn.aaai.org/FLAIRS/2005/Flairs05-085.pdf

items.text: Point out an error with a question that lets them see it rather than a correction, without implying the answer is right. Praise the solution, not the person.
items.attribution: Lepper, M. R., & Woolverton, M. (2002). The wisdom of practice: Lessons learned from the study of highly effective tutors. In J. Aronson (Ed.), Improving academic achievement (pp. 135-158). Academic Press. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-012064455-1/50010-5

items.text: Watch how they feel as well as what they know: if they sound discouraged, say so briefly and give them something next that they can succeed at.
items.attribution: Lepper, M. R., & Woolverton, M. (2002). The wisdom of practice: Lessons learned from the study of highly effective tutors. In J. Aronson (Ed.), Improving academic achievement (pp. 135-158). Academic Press. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-012064455-1/50010-5 D'Mello, S., & Graesser, A. (2012). Dynamics of affective states during complex learning. Learning and Instruction, 22(2), 145-157. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2011.10.001

items.text: Save the back-and-forth for what is hard for this learner. If it is within easy reach, let them get on with it rather than drawing it out.
items.attribution: VanLehn, K., Graesser, A. C., Jackson, G. T., Jordan, P., Olney, A., & Rosé, C. P. (2007). When are tutorial dialogues more effective than reading? Cognitive Science, 31(1), 3-62. https://doi.org/10.1080/03640210709336984

cite: VIABLE Lab (2026). Tutoring talk: guidance from research. The wording is VIABLE Lab's; each piece names the studies it draws on.
attribution: Wording by VIABLE Lab, CC BY 4.0. The findings belong to the researchers each piece cites.

evidence.original: Tutoring works: human tutoring d = 0.79 and step-based computer tutors d = 0.76 against no tutoring, well below the often-quoted 2 sigma (VanLehn, 2011); pre-K to 12 field experiments pool at 0.288 SD (Nickow et al., 2024). Which talk causes this is less clear. With tutors barred from explaining, students learned as well from prompts (Chi et al., 2001). Dialogue beat reading only when novices studied material written for intermediates, in qualitative physics (VanLehn et al., 2007). Expectation and misconception tailored dialogue comes from AutoTutor, modeled on human tutors, with gains near 0.8 sigma in its authors' own evaluations (Graesser et al., 2005; Graesser, Chipman et al., 2005; Nye et al., 2014). The expert-tutor account is observational, from experienced primary and secondary math tutors (Lepper & Woolverton, 2002). Talk moves come from whole-class teaching, not one-on-one, and taking them up at scale is hard (Michaels et al., 2008; Michaels & O'Connor, 2012; O'Connor & Michaels, 2019). In 72 classrooms, ages 10-11, elaborating and querying went with higher mastery where students participated widely, a correlation (Howe et al., 2019). A school trial of dialogic teaching, 76 schools, found about 2 months' gain (EEF, 2017). Automated feedback raised instructors' uptake of student ideas by 13% in a trial of 1,136 instructors, with only suggestive effects on students (Demszky et al., 2024). How large formative assessment's effect is remains disputed (Black & Wiliam, 1998; Kingston & Nash, 2011; Briggs et al., 2012).
evidence.integration: Not yet compared with and without it in this harness.
evidence.unknown: Talk moves were built for teachers with whole classes, and tutoring studies measure human tutors or scripted systems. Nobody has shown that a language model told to revoice, press for reasons or tailor to misconceptions teaches better for it. Whether learners take a model's questions as genuine interest or as withholding is open. Reading how someone feels from a few typed lines is unreliable.

risk_notes: Its text goes to a model as guidance. Nothing runs and nothing about a learner goes anywhere. What the teacher set for how far to go comes first. Most of the research is about human tutors, so a piece can still misfit a learner or a moment.
